variants.name: Interface-constrained generic policy (classic .NET)
variants.idiom_name: generic host constrained to a policy interface (where TPolicy : IPolicy)
variants.implementation_notes: C#'s local idiom is a generic host whose policy parameter is a type constrained to an interface that states the contract (sealed class Cache<K, V, TPolicy> where TPolicy : IEvictionPolicy<K>, new()); the policy is a type argument, so every binding is a distinct closed generic type and the compiler checks conformance. Members are reached through the constraint, and because the CLR only specializes generic instantiations over value types, reference-type policies keep virtual dispatch - 'zero cost' is not portable. Policy enrichment must be written out: extension methods with the same constraint or explicit forwarding members replace the classic inheritance-based enrichment, and when the variant becomes a runtime decision, inject an interface implementation instead (Strategy/dependency injection).
pitfalls: Reference-type policies keep virtual dispatch: the JIT specializes generic instantiations only over value types, so a class policy pays the same call cost as an injected object.

Constraints accept only declared interfaces and base classes: a policy cannot provide extra members the host discovers (no duck typing, no enrichment), so anything beyond the interface must be forwarded explicitly.
`new()` in the constraint forces a parameterless constructor and hides construction cost; inject a policy instance or a factory method instead when policies need configuration.

variants.name: Static abstract interface members as a policy contract (C# 11)
variants.idiom_name: where T : IPolicy<TSelf> with static abstract members (generic math style)
variants.implementation_notes: C# 11 lets an interface declare static abstract members, so a policy contract can require static methods, operators and properties and the host can call them through a constrained type parameter (T.Pick(...)) with the implementation resolved from the type argument at compile time - the mechanism behind .NET 7's INumber<TSelf> generic math interfaces. This is the closest C# comes to a genuine compile-time policy: no policy instance is needed and value-type policies are devirtualized, at the price of the self-referential CRTP-like constraint (TSelf : IPolicy<TSelf>) and of the fact that static members are unreachable through the interface itself.
pitfalls: Static abstract members cannot be invoked on an instance or on the interface itself (IEvictionPolicy<int>.Pick is invalid); they are only reachable through a constrained type parameter.
Only value-type (struct) policies gain static dispatch in practice - a class policy reintroduces virtual dispatch through the interface, so mixing the two forms erases the advantage.
